subject: Longitudinal pooled logistic, causal modeling, measurement error

messages.author: ff9524505ae379dc
messages.subject: Longitudinal pooled logistic, causal modeling, measurement error
parts:
I need help with a complex model that has some parts I can't seem to optimize.

The goal of my code: I am trying to fit multiple longitudinal (time-pooled) logistic models to estimate a discrete hazard function for two mutually exclusive, terminal events (2 causes of death). The hazard functions are then used to calculate cumulative risk of each cause. This requires 3 or 4 models, depending on the problem. I model each cause of death, as well as one primary time-varying exposure (continuous) and a secondary  time-varying exposure (binary) that is correlated with the first one.

My data: a data set with ~ 27,000 observations, each corresponding to one person-year, along with a binary indicator of death and the two exposures. There are ~90 events of type 1 and ~500 of type 2. All told, I have about 50 parameters (12 for each event model, 16 and 20 for the two risk factor models). In my field, the events are usually modeled as a function of cumulative exposure (among other things).

Problem 1: getting the model to converge in a timely fashion
Problem 2: also correcting for measurement error

I have had a stan model running on a server for two days.The following traceplot is the output of cumulative risk after a burnin of 1000 iterations. I expected slow, but I did not expect such poor MCMC. The traceplots for other parameters look equally abysmal. For reference, the posterior mean should be around 0.08.


I made a simulation that captures the important parts of the model without being too complex. This includes correcting for measurement error that is assumed to be Berkson error. The above trace plot is basically this model, but without correcting for measurement error. The simulation model seems to return much better looking trace plots, but is still slow. The real example includes two additional models, neither of which can be done without looping over observations.



// model implied by the data generating mechanism in the simulation
// standardizing all independent variables
data{
  int N;
  int d1[N];
  int d2[N];
  vector[N] mx;
  vector[N] z;
  vector[N] tms;
  vector[N] id;
}
transformed data{
  vector[N] tms2;
  vector[N] tms3;  
  tms2 <- tms .* tms;
  tms3 <- tms .* tms2;

}
parameters{
  real b0;
  vector[8] b;
  real c0;
  vector[8] c;
  vector<lower=0>[N] berk_err; // multiplicative measurement error
}
model{
  { // local environment
  vector[N] cx_cor;
  vector[N] cx_cor2;
  vector[N] cx_cor3;
  vector[N] cx_corz;
  // measurement model (assumed multiplicative berkson error): 
  //   E(log(true_exposure) | measured_exposure) = log(measured_exposure)
    berk_err ~ lognormal(0, log(5./4.));
  //increment_log_prob(-(log(berk_err)));
  // cumulative exposure
  for(i in 1:N){
    if(i != 1 && id[i] == id[i-1]) cx_cor[i] <- cx_cor[i-1] + mx[i]*berk_err[i];
    else cx_cor[i] <- mx[i]*berk_err[i];}
  cx_cor2 <- cx_cor .* cx_cor;
  cx_cor3 <- cx_cor .* cx_cor2;
  cx_corz <- cx_cor .* z; 
  b0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  b  ~ normal(0, 3);
  c0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
  c  ~ normal(0, 3);
  // discrete, cause-specific hazard models
  d1  ~ bernoulli_logit(b0 + b[1]*tms + b[2]*tms2 + b[3]*tms3 +
                        b[4]*cx_cor2 + b[5]*cx_cor3 +
                        b[6]*cx_cor + b[7]*z + b[8]*cx_corz);
  
  d2  ~ bernoulli_logit(c0 + c[1]*tms + c[2]*tms2 + c[3]*tms3 +
                        c[4]*cx_cor2 + c[5]*cx_cor3 +
                        c[6]*cx_cor + c[7]*z + c[8]*cx_corz);}
  // a model for E(log(x)|z,time, past x) and a model for logit(z| past x, time) go here
}
generated quantities{
// calculate cumulative risk here under different exposure scenarios
}


One key part of this that I am fairly certain is slowing this down is that there is a loop due to my need to model death as a function of cumulative exposure. However, even under having things mostly vectorized, the model still a) runs too slow and b) is not converging. If I could solve problem (b) I would be happy. The component models all run quickly and without errors/warnings in the `glm` function in R.


For completeness, here is code to simulate the data in R.

dgm <- function(N, maxT){
  set.seed(7826)
  data = matrix(NA, nrow=N*maxT, ncol=9)
  row = 0
  for(id in 1:N){
    cx = 0
    mcx = 0
    hasdied = 0
    for(tm in 1:maxT){
      row = row + 1
      # true exposure at time t
      t10= tm/10
      truex = exp(rnorm(1, -1 + -0.1*tm, .3))
      berkson_error = exp(rnorm(1, 0,log(5/4)))
      cx = cx + truex
      mx = truex*berkson_error
      mcx = mcx + mcx
      z = rbinom(1, 1, 1/(1+exp(-(-0.5 + cx))))
      # two causes of death
      logit1 = -7.5 + 0.035*t10 - 0.0025*t10**2 + 0.00125*t10**3 + 0.05*cx  + 
                0.005*cx**2 + 0.00025*cx**3 + z - 0.025*z*cx
      logit2 = -6 + 0.035*t10 - 0.0025*t10**2 + 0.00125*t10**3 + 0.05*cx  + 
                0.005*cx**2 + 0.00025*cx**3 + z - 0.025*z*cx
      # causes of death
      d1 = rbinom(1, 1, 1/(1+exp(-logit1)))
      d2 = ifelse(d1==1, 0, rbinom(1, 1, 1/(1+exp(-logit2))))
      data[row, ] = c(id, tm, mcx, mx, cx, z, d1, d2, hasdied)
      if(d1 | d2) hasdied = 1
    }}
 ret = data.frame(data[data[,9]==0, 1:8])
 names(ret) <- c('id', 'tm', 'mcx', 'mx', 'cx', 'z', 'd1', 'd2')
 ret
}

dat = dgm(1000,60)

I know the following problems are occurring:
 - the need to model time 'flexibly' by including polynomial or spline terms leads to some parameter correlation in the posterior (but not too bad, see figure below for the worst example I could find in the limited runs I have - most pairwise plots gave a nice circular cloud of points).
 - there is likely separation in at least one of the logistic models, though R gives no warnings

I have tried the following things in an effort to speed this up:
 - standardizing/unstandardizing all variables on the RHS of the models
 - vectorizing/unvectorizing the probability models when possible
 - modeling the berkson error as `log(berk_err) ~ normal()`, rather than `berk_err ~ lognormal()`
 - strengthening priors on the regression coefficient parameters (down to normal(0, 0.1))
 - going to a simpler set of models with fewer parameters (this is not really justifiable, and it doesn't really seem to be fixing the problem).
 - moving the multiplication to create polynomial terms into/out of the RHS of the model and into/out of the transformed data block or other parts of the model block
 
This seems like it should be going faster AND converging because:
 - this is a relatively fast problem to solve in frequentist-land (aside from measurement error) - the part that takes the longest is calculating the cumulative risk after fitting the models
 - the joint model is complex, but it's just made of standard linear or logistic regression problems that don't depend on one another (until introducing measurement error, of course)

I'm happy for any suggestions, with or without consideration for the measurement error correction.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Longitudinal pooled logistic, causal modeling, measurement error
parts:
I don't understand the model (my fault, not saying it's bad), but
it does look like it's coded efficiently in Stan. It looks like
things are converging other than b0 and b[1:8] judging from the followup
post, just slowly.

That's usually a sign of non-identifiability. b0 shows up here:

> parameters{
> real b0;
...
> b0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

> d1 ~ bernoulli_logit(b0 + b[1]*tms + b[2]*tms2 + b[3]*tms3 +
> b[4]*cx_cor2 + b[5]*cx_cor3 +
> b[6]*cx_cor + b[7]*z + b[8]*cx_corz);

Even though I haven't dug into the specifics, my guess is that you're
getting strong correlations among b0 and b[1:8]. You can use pairs()
to try to plot (just restrict to b0 and b).

What is your treedepth like? If it's high, it means there's a lot of
nasty curvature and Stan's having to use a very small step size.
Usually the only way around that is reparameterization.

- Bob

> On Jun 18, 2016, at 12:35 AM, Alex Keil <alex...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I need help with a complex model that has some parts I can't seem to optimize.
>
> The goal of my code: I am trying to fit multiple longitudinal (time-pooled) logistic models to estimate a discrete hazard function for two mutually exclusive, terminal events (2 causes of death). The hazard functions are then used to calculate cumulative risk of each cause. This requires 3 or 4 models, depending on the problem. I model each cause of death, as well as one primary time-varying exposure (continuous) and a secondary time-varying exposure (binary) that is correlated with the first one.
>
> My data: a data set with ~ 27,000 observations, each corresponding to one person-year, along with a binary indicator of death and the two exposures. There are ~90 events of type 1 and ~500 of type 2. All told, I have about 50 parameters (12 for each event model, 16 and 20 for the two risk factor models). In my field, the events are usually modeled as a function of cumulative exposure (among other things).
>
> Problem 1: getting the model to converge in a timely fashion
> Problem 2: also correcting for measurement error
>
> I have had a stan model running on a server for two days.The following traceplot is the output of cumulative risk after a burnin of 1000 iterations. I expected slow, but I did not expect such poor MCMC. The traceplots for other parameters look equally abysmal. For reference, the posterior mean should be around 0.08.
>
>
>
>

> I made a simulation that captures the important parts of the model without being too complex. This includes correcting for measurement error that is assumed to be Berkson error. The above trace plot is basically this model, but without correcting for measurement error. The simulation model seems to return much better looking trace plots, but is still slow. The real example includes two additional models, neither of which can be done without looping over observations.
>
>
>
>
>
> // model implied by the data generating mechanism in the simulation
> // standardizing all independent variables
> data{
> int N;
> int d1[N];
> int d2[N];
> vector[N] mx;
> vector[N] z;
> vector[N] tms;
> vector[N] id;
> }
> transformed data{
> vector[N] tms2;
> vector[N] tms3;
> tms2 <- tms .* tms;
> tms3 <- tms .* tms2;
>
> }
> parameters{
> real b0;
> vector[8] b;
> real c0;
> vector[8] c;
> vector<lower=0>[N] berk_err; // multiplicative measurement error
> }
> model{
> { // local environment
> vector[N] cx_cor;
> vector[N] cx_cor2;
> vector[N] cx_cor3;
> vector[N] cx_corz;
> // measurement model (assumed multiplicative berkson error):
> // E(log(true_exposure) | measured_exposure) = log(measured_exposure)
> berk_err ~ lognormal(0, log(5./4.));
> //increment_log_prob(-(log(berk_err)));
> // cumulative exposure
> for(i in 1:N){
> if(i != 1 && id[i] == id[i-1]) cx_cor[i] <- cx_cor[i-1] + mx[i]*berk_err[i];
> else cx_cor[i] <- mx[i]*berk_err[i];}
> cx_cor2 <- cx_cor .* cx_cor;
> cx_cor3 <- cx_cor .* cx_cor2;
> cx_corz <- cx_cor .* z;
> b0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> b ~ normal(0, 3);
> c0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> c ~ normal(0, 3);
> // discrete, cause-specific hazard models
> d1 ~ bernoulli_logit(b0 + b[1]*tms + b[2]*tms2 + b[3]*tms3 +
> b[4]*cx_cor2 + b[5]*cx_cor3 +
> b[6]*cx_cor + b[7]*z + b[8]*cx_corz);
>
> d2 ~ bernoulli_logit(c0 + c[1]*tms + c[2]*tms2 + c[3]*tms3 +
> c[4]*cx_cor2 + c[5]*cx_cor3 +
> c[6]*cx_cor + c[7]*z + c[8]*cx_corz);}
> // a model for E(log(x)|z,time, past x) and a model for logit(z| past x, time) go here
> }
> generated quantities{
> // calculate cumulative risk here under different exposure scenarios
> }
>
> One key part of this that I am fairly certain is slowing this down is that there is a loop due to my need to model death as a function of cumulative exposure. However, even under having things mostly vectorized, the model still a) runs too slow and b) is not converging. If I could solve problem (b) I would be happy. The component models all run quickly and without errors/warnings in the `glm` function in R.
>
>
> For completeness, here is code to simulate the data in R.
>
> dgm <- function(N, maxT){
> set.seed(7826)
> data = matrix(NA, nrow=N*maxT, ncol=9)
> row = 0
> for(id in 1:N){
> cx = 0
> mcx = 0
> hasdied = 0
> for(tm in 1:maxT){
> row = row + 1
> # true exposure at time t
> t10= tm/10
> truex = exp(rnorm(1, -1 + -0.1*tm, .3))
> berkson_error = exp(rnorm(1, 0,log(5/4)))
> cx = cx + truex
> mx = truex*berkson_error
> mcx = mcx + mcx
> z = rbinom(1, 1, 1/(1+exp(-(-0.5 + cx))))
> # two causes of death
> logit1 = -7.5 + 0.035*t10 - 0.0025*t10**2 + 0.00125*t10**3 + 0.05*cx +
> 0.005*cx**2 + 0.00025*cx**3 + z - 0.025*z*cx
> logit2 = -6 + 0.035*t10 - 0.0025*t10**2 + 0.00125*t10**3 + 0.05*cx +
> 0.005*cx**2 + 0.00025*cx**3 + z - 0.025*z*cx
> # causes of death
> d1 = rbinom(1, 1, 1/(1+exp(-logit1)))
> d2 = ifelse(d1==1, 0, rbinom(1, 1, 1/(1+exp(-logit2))))
> data[row, ] = c(id, tm, mcx, mx, cx, z, d1, d2, hasdied)
> if(d1 | d2) hasdied = 1
> }}
> ret = data.frame(data[data[,9]==0, 1:8])
> names(ret) <- c('id', 'tm', 'mcx', 'mx', 'cx', 'z', 'd1', 'd2')
> ret
> }
>
> dat = dgm(1000,60)
>
> I know the following problems are occurring:
> - the need to model time 'flexibly' by including polynomial or spline terms leads to some parameter correlation in the posterior (but not too bad, see figure below for the worst example I could find in the limited runs I have - most pairwise plots gave a nice circular cloud of points).
> - there is likely separation in at least one of the logistic models, though R gives no warnings
>
>
>

> I have tried the following things in an effort to speed this up:
> - standardizing/unstandardizing all variables on the RHS of the models
> - vectorizing/unvectorizing the probability models when possible
> - modeling the berkson error as `log(berk_err) ~ normal()`, rather than `berk_err ~ lognormal()`
> - strengthening priors on the regression coefficient parameters (down to normal(0, 0.1))
> - going to a simpler set of models with fewer parameters (this is not really justifiable, and it doesn't really seem to be fixing the problem).
> - moving the multiplication to create polynomial terms into/out of the RHS of the model and into/out of the transformed data block or other parts of the model block
>
> This seems like it should be going faster AND converging because:
> - this is a relatively fast problem to solve in frequentist-land (aside from measurement error) - the part that takes the longest is calculating the cumulative risk after fitting the models
> - the joint model is complex, but it's just made of standard linear or logistic regression problems that don't depend on one another (until introducing measurement error, of course)
>
> I'm happy for any suggestions, with or without consideration for the measurement error correction.
>
>

parts:
Thanks for taking a look.

The overall model can be separated into 3 tasks: fitting two logistic models and one log-linear model simultaneously. It's an epidemiology problem, dealing with time-dependent risk-factors for mortality. One dependent variable is a mortality outcome, and one is a discrete time-to-event outcome, where I am modeling a discrete hazard for switching from treatment to another. This second model is only fit to a subset of the data (i.e. you are "censored" when you switch treatments). The data structure is that one observation is equal to one year per person, so there are multiple records per person. The simulation i had posted was a simplified version of this where I did not model treatment switching.

I'm getting a treedepth that averages from 7 to 11, with stepsize that is approx 10^-3 for one model and approx 10^-6 for another that includes correction for measurement error (where I know there is non-identifiability). I understand the latter stepsize, at least, is quite poor.

The bivariate scatter plots that included model intercept for one of the causes of death looked good for the most part. I've included 2 from my actual example without measurement error- the one that looks like the parameters are fairly independent is what I would a typical scatter plot. The other plot that shows strong correlation is atypical, but occurs for one variable. The variable happens to be my main treatment of interest, so I can't just exclude it. The third plot is from the model in which I also try to correct for measurement error - obviously, this one is horrible, but I don't feel like I can really address this one until I get the simpler case working more efficiently.

I'm using a restricted, cubic spline with fixed knots to characterize my treatment (it's a standardized, continuous variable). I could move to something else like a cubic polynomial function, but I'm guessing I will have the same problem. I'm open to suggestions on how I could have a flexible, non-linear function on a continuous variable that won't suffer these problems.

I'm stumped re: reparameterization. A while ago, I found a list of things to try with slow logistic models in STAN, but I can't seem to find that again - I recall trying a number of things from that list, but nothing made this magically start working. I took a look at things like the "matt trick," but I didn't quite see how that would work here. Would I just use it with the variables that have the highest posterior correlation with the intercept terms? I'm happy for any suggestions.
